role: Lifeguard at a sports center natatorium
headline: Retired from a sports school swim team, now a pool lifeguard at a sports center in Qingdao, sitting the high chair, testing chlorine and watching the heads of hundreds of swimmers every day, and lent out to the bathing beaches in summer
unit: A municipal sports center in Qingdao with a swimming and diving hall, a stadium and an indoor arena; the pool is open to the public and hosts classes and competitions all year
education: Secondary sports school (swimming), later the national lifeguard qualification
level: You still swim the 400 meters freestyle in under seven minutes, hold your lifeguard and first-aid certificates, and have water tows and CPR down cold. The venue's inspection sheets, water quality logs and emergency plans, you've only just started learning to write
intro: You soaked in sports school pools for eight years and missed the provincial team by a whisker. The year you retired, you got your lifeguard certificate and joined the natatorium at this sports center. Now you sit on a lifeguard chair two meters up, below you fifty meters and eight lanes of water, and every day hundreds of heads bob up and down in it. As of today, how fast you swim no longer matters; what matters is how sharply you see.
salary_note: Estimate: lifeguards and safety attendants at a Qingdao municipal sports center earn base pay plus night-session and event allowances, a little below the national figure. Summer secondments to the bathing beaches pay extra; in winter, with fewer swimmers, the allowances shrink too.

facts.label: Venue Patroller / Pool Lifeguard (current level)
facts.value: 0-2 years, ¥4,420–6,500 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Handling a swimmer's sudden cardiac arrest

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Doing a safety round before the venue opens

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Before opening you get in first and swim a lap along the bottom, checking for dropped objects and loose tiles. Out again, you test free chlorine and pH with the test kit and write them on the water quality board.

The morning swimmers arrive on the dot, mostly in their sixties and seventies, steadier in the water than the young. One old man tells you the same thing every day: young fellow, the water's a bit cold today.
Up on the chair your eyes sweep by zone: deep end, shallow end, starting blocks, poolside. Twenty seconds a sweep, and what you watch is heads, not hands.
Off rotation, you inspect the floors, handrails and non-slip mats in the changing rooms and showers, tick the inspection sheet, and report a loose socket on a hair dryer for repair.
Lunch in the canteen: mackerel dumplings. A coworker says there are two children's classes this afternoon, forty-odd kids, and the shallow end needs one more guard.

A child swallows water in the shallow end and clings to the edge crying. You jump in, lift him out, pat his back, check his color, ask him questions, hand him to his mother, and go back to write a line in the log.
The night session is busy, wave after wave of young people off work. You stand at the deep end checking deep-water certificates, and one man doesn't have one; you ask him to go to the shallow end.

Clearing the pool. You walk the deck once, checking the water, the bottom, the changing rooms, and turn off the lights only when the last person has gone. Riding home, the wind off the sea tastes of salt.

ladder.title: Venue Patroller / Pool Lifeguard
ladder.focus: Patrol, stand guard, learn first aid and fire safety.

ladder.title: Sports Venue Safety Attendant
ladder.focus: Run daily safety rounds to standard, record hazards and hold emergency drills.

ladder.title: Safety Supervisor
ladder.focus: Safety plans for large events, rostering and training, and dealing with inspections.

ladder.title: Venue Operations Manager (Safety)
ladder.focus: The venue's whole safety system, risk assessment and compliance.

ladder.title: Venue General Manager / Director of Safety

ai_tasks.name: Doing a safety round before the venue opens
ai_tasks.how: AI can use electronic checklists, cameras and sensors to flag common hazards and log them automatically. A person has to go and look, touch and try things on site, and judge whether a facility is really fit to use.

ai_tasks.name: Checking lifeguard staffing and certification
ai_tasks.how: AI can check the certificate register, flag expiries and find staffing gaps against the roster. A person only needs to spot-check weekly that lifeguards are really on post and positioned where they should be.

ai_tasks.name: Running a drowning emergency drill
ai_tasks.how: AI can write the drill script, design scenarios and generate the evaluation form and debrief record. A person organizes it on site, leads the drill and corrects technique.

ai_tasks.name: Writing a safety plan for a 3,000-person event and applying for the permit
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft the plan from a template, check the clauses and lay out crowd flows and posts. A person settles the plan, works it through with the police, and signs for the result.

ai_tasks.name: Handling a swimmer's sudden cardiac arrest
ai_tasks.how: A person has to start CPR on the spot, use the AED, call emergency services and keep the people around calm. At most AI can prompt the steps; it can't do the hands-on part.

ai_tasks.name: Getting ready for a safety inspection by the sports authority
ai_tasks.how: AI can organize the ledgers and records and produce a self-check list against the inspection standards. A person faces the inspection on site, explains the situation and carries out the fixes.

ai_tasks.name: Directing the crowd out after an event
ai_tasks.how: AI can monitor crowd density through cameras and raise warnings. A person, in a noisy venue, uses voice, gestures and position to direct ten thousand people out in order, adapting all the time.

ai_tasks.name: Doing the venue's annual risk assessment and insurance plan
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile past incident and hazard records, draft the assessment and compare insurance terms. A person judges the real risks, explains them to management and recommends what to insure.

events.e_first_rescue: In the deep end a middle-aged man suddenly stops moving, floating face down. You leap from the chair and have him at the edge in a dozen seconds, a coworker already running over with the AED. He coughs up some water and comes round. That night you sit alone in the changing room for a long time.
events.e_miss: Your attention slips during a sweep, and a child slides into the deep end right under your nose; it's the old lifeguard on the next chair who sees him first. The boy is fine, and your supervisor has you go over the technique of zone scanning at the morning briefing.
events.e_beach: In summer you're lent out to a bathing beach, standing on the sand ten hours a day, shouting yourself hoarse, your back peeling. Once you go in and tow back a swimmer carried out by a rip current, and when you reach the shore your legs are jelly.
events.e_chlorine: Years in chlorinated water and air, and your hair turns yellowish, your skin dry, your eyes red by every afternoon. You start tucking a bottle of eye drops into your bag every day.
events.e_old_man: The old man who says the water's cold every day stays away for a month. Then his daughter comes to the pool to say he was in hospital for a while, he's fine now, and he asked her to come tell you.
events.e_love: One of the coaches for the children's classes comes over to the chair for a few words after every lesson. Later the two of you climb Mount Lao together, and on the way down she says you were watching people the whole way up the mountain too.
events.e_ai_drown: The pool installs an AI anti-drowning system, underwater cameras plus an algorithm: if someone stays still on the bottom for more than ten seconds, the band on the lifeguard's wrist vibrates. In its first month it goes off more than thirty times, mostly for kids holding their breath on the bottom for fun.
events.e_cert_safety: You pass the social sports instructor certificate and the fire safety management training, and organize a full evacuation drill of the hall on your own for the first time: from the alarm to the last person out, four minutes.
events.e_beer_fest: During the beer festival the square outside the sports center is packed, and you're seconded to crowd control, standing at one crossing two nights running, a glow stick in your hand.
events.e_inspection: The city sports authority inspects the pool's opening conditions: lifeguard ratios, water quality logs, first-aid equipment, warning signs. You lay out the ledgers one by one, and the inspection team marks everything top grade.
events.e_shoulder: The shoulder injury from your sports school years flares up. Towing someone once, a stab of pain shoots through your shoulder halfway. You grit your teeth and get them to the edge, and for three weeks after you can't lift your arm.
events.e_wedding: You get married in Qingdao, and your coworkers at the pool give you a life ring covered in their signatures. You hang it on the wall of your new home.
events.e_event: The sports center hosts a national swimming competition, and you're responsible for venue safety during the meet. In three days you walk dozens of kilometers between the stands, the corridors and the call room.
events.e_cardiac: A night-session swimmer suddenly collapses at the poolside in cardiac arrest. You and a coworker take turns with compressions, use the AED, call emergency services, and keep going until the ambulance arrives. When they carry him out he has a pulse. Your hands shake all night.
events.e_baby: Your daughter is born. At six months old you carry her into the children's pool for the first time; she slaps the water and laughs, and your hand never leaves the back of her head.
events.e_typhoon: The day before a typhoon makes landfall, you and your coworkers reinforce the stadium's temporary stands and billboards one by one and cut power to everything outdoors. That night you sleep in the duty room at the hall.
events.e_ai_patrol: Venue rounds switch to electronic checklists and sensors, and the system pushes alerts for wherever there's a leak or a door left open. You go from walking a lap with a notebook to taking a tablet to verify the few items the system reports.
events.e_mentor: A new lifeguard you trained makes his first rescue on his own, and when he comes out his hands are still shaking. He says: I wasn't thinking about anything, I just did what you said, watch the head first.
events.e_concert: The stadium hosts a concert for thirty thousand, and you're one of the authors of the safety plan. As the crowd leaves you stand on high ground over the main concourse calling through a megaphone over and over, and the crowd flows slowly out like water.
events.e_parent: Your mother goes into hospital back home in Weifang, and you take a week off. The ward's care worker asks what you do; you say lifeguard, and she says then teach me how to do CPR.
events.e_age: After forty you get in the water less and less. The young lifeguards swim faster than you, but when someone in the water isn't right, it's often you who sees it first.
events.e_system: The venue safety management manual you led the writing of is rolled out by the city to more than a dozen public pools. When a new pool opens, the first copy handed out is that one.

c_beach_or_pool.title: Go to the bathing beach this summer or not
c_beach_or_pool.situation: The beach lifeguard team is short-handed, and the sports center asks who'll be lent out for the whole summer. The sea has rip currents, hidden rocks and tourists who swim after drinking, and the allowance is double; summer is the busiest time at the pool too, and whoever stays can learn more about running the venue.

options.label: Go to the beach
options.result: You stand on the sand all summer and learn to read rip currents from the color of the sea. You come back so dark your coworkers barely recognize you, with twenty-odd old lifeguards' numbers in your phone.

options.label: Stay at the pool
options.result: You stay and learn to write inspection sheets and emergency plans under your supervisor. Summer night sessions bring over a thousand people an evening, and you stand at the deep end the whole time.

c_safety_officer.title: Move up to Sports Venue Safety Attendant
c_safety_officer.situation: The sports center wants to move one lifeguard into a venue safety attendant post, covering not just the pool but daily rounds, hazard records and emergency drills for the whole center. You'd need fire safety and first-aid training certificates and to learn to keep ledgers, and you'd spend a lot less time on the chair.

options.label: Apply for the move
options.result: After work you go to fire safety classes, and on weekends you go through the venue against the standards clause by clause. When you hand in your first hazard list, your supervisor says you were more thorough than he is.

options.label: Stay on the chair
options.result: You say you like being by the water. The post goes to someone else, and you sit the chair two more years, your eyes getting sharper and sharper.

c_coach.title: Become a coach at a swim school
c_coach.situation: An older teammate from sports school has opened a swim school for children and wants you as a coach. In a summer holiday month the classes pay double what you earn now, and winter has few lessons; instead of watching hundreds of people, you'd watch a dozen kids.

options.label: Become a coach
options.result: The first thing you teach in your first lesson isn't breaststroke but how to float and how to shout for help.
options.end: You became a swim coach, teaching a hundred-odd children a summer not to be afraid of water. You always teach them to float in the first lesson, and tell them that if you can float, the water can't take you.

options.label: Stay at the venue
options.result: You say the venue is steady, with full benefits. Your teammate says come help a few days when summer gets too busy, and you say sure.

options.label: Teach a few classes on weekends
options.result: Every weekend you teach four classes at your teammate's school, ¥2,000 more a month. On Monday mornings, climbing onto the chair, your legs feel heavy.

c_ai_drill.title: Learn to design the procedure for AI alerts and human response
c_ai_drill.situation: With more anti-drowning systems and camera alerts, the sports center wants someone to design how people and machines work together: who moves first when the band vibrates, what to do when the system is down, which alerts need checking on the spot. Your supervisor wants you to lead it, but some say the pool will cut lifeguard posts afterward.

options.label: Lead the procedure
options.result: You turn every kind of danger you've seen in the water into a response rule, and spell out where people stand when the system fails. On the day of the drill, from the band vibrating to the person at the edge, twenty seconds.

options.label: Stick to your own post
options.result: You say alarm or no alarm, you still have to watch the water. Someone else writes the procedure; there's one rule you think is wrong, and you raise it at a meeting.

c_supervisor.title: Compete for Safety Supervisor
c_supervisor.situation: The sports center is naming a Safety Supervisor to handle rostering and training for all its lifeguards and safety staff, write the safety plans for large events and deal with police and fire inspections. To compete you present an emergency you handled and a safety plan for a 3,000-person event.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: You talk about the night-session swimmer who collapsed at the poolside, from the first compression to the ambulance pulling away. A panelist asks how your plan handles the crowd leaving, and you draw a diagram.

options.label: Leave it to an older colleague
options.result: You think old Han, with twenty years at the pool, is better suited, and don't apply. Once he has the job, the hard summer rosters always go to you first.

c_event_security.title: Join an event security company
c_event_security.situation: A company that does security for big sporting events and concerts wants to poach you as a security manager, traveling the country for forty percent more pay. Marathons, concerts, sailing regattas: dozens of events a year, each one tens of thousands of people.

options.label: Join the security company
options.result: With a radio and a stack of safety plans, you board a high-speed train out of town.
options.end: You became an event security manager, drawing evacuation routes in stadium after stadium and directing the crowds out from high ground. Every time tens of thousands of people walk out safely, you sit a while in the empty stands.

options.label: Stay at the sports center
options.result: You say your child is still small and you don't want to be on the road all year. The company says they'll call you in for big events, and you say fine.

c_manager.title: Become Venue Operations Manager (Safety)
c_manager.situation: The sports center is promoting a venue operations manager to run the natatorium and indoor arena as a whole: the safety system, risk assessment and insurance. Taking it means meetings, reports and approvals, and rarely standing at the poolside again.

options.label: Take the operations manager job
options.result: You start chairing morning meetings, reviewing budgets and negotiating terms with insurers, a pile of risk assessments on your desk. The last time you sat the lifeguard chair was three months ago, covering for someone on sick leave.

options.label: You'd rather run safety
options.result: You turn it down, saying you're better on the floor. The new manager arrives, and before every big event he comes to go through the plan with you first.

c_hometown.title: Go back to the new sports hall in Weifang
c_hometown.situation: Your hometown of Weifang has built a new public fitness center and needs someone who knows venue safety to be its safety supervisor: twenty percent less pay, ten minutes from your parents. Your child is in school in Qingdao, and your wife works in Qingdao.

options.label: Go to Weifang
options.result: You go back alone first and drive to Qingdao on weekends. Everything at the new center is new, and the lifeguards are kids fresh from their certificates.

options.label: Stay in Qingdao
options.result: You say keeping the family together matters most. You go back to Weifang once a month, and install handrails and non-slip mats in your parents' new flat.

c_gm.title: Become Director of Safety for the sports centers
c_gm.situation: The city is merging several sports centers into one group and wants a director of safety to oversee safety operations at every venue. You'd deal with the sports authority, police, fire services and insurers, and whatever happens, you're the first one asked.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You start traveling between venues, and before every new pool opens, you get in and swim a lap of the bottom yourself.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend a supervisor you trained. The first call he makes after taking over is to ask where the lifeguard chairs should go at a new pool.

endings.retire: On your last day you get into the water once more before opening and swim slowly along the bottom. The tiles are the same tiles, the black line on the bottom the same black line. You climb out, dry off, and watch a young lifeguard climb onto the chair and wave to you. You wave back, then turn and test the chlorine one more time.
endings.burnout: That summer your shoulder and back give out together, and you can no longer tow someone through the water; the doctor says no more lifeguard chair. The sports center moves you to equipment management in the indoor arena, regular hours. Passing the natatorium, you still glance through the glass at the deep end.

stages: You keep the two-meter lifeguard chair and the stretch of water below it. Every day before opening you test the chlorine and check the bottom, on the chair you sweep your zone every twenty seconds, off rotation you inspect the changing rooms, check deep-water certificates and fill in the duty log; when there's danger, you're the first one in. The supervisor and the old lifeguards set the rules and you follow them; do it right and no one praises you, do it wrong and the whole pool knows.

You've come down off the chair and now handle daily safety for the whole sports center. Every day you walk the natatorium, the arena and the stadium with a checklist, recording hazards, reporting repairs and chasing fixes; every quarter you run an emergency drill and write the debrief; at events you're responsible for one zone's crowd. You now hold the fire equipment register and access to the camera playback.

You are the sports center's safety supervisor, in charge of rostering and training for twenty-odd lifeguards and safety staff. Before big events you write the safety plan and submit it to the police for approval, and on the day you stand at the command post; when sports, police or fire authorities inspect, you're the one answering. Tens of thousands of people come in and go out by the plan you signed.

You run operations across several venues, and safety is the first page you look at. Every week you chair the operations meeting, reviewing attendance, incident and hazard records, budgets, insurance and the annual risk assessment; you report to the sports authority, and you explain to management why a particular expense can't be cut. You rarely get in the water now; what you hold is reports and contracts.

What you set now is how several of the city's sports centers stay safe: the management manual, staffing levels, training and assessment, the emergency system. Half your week is meetings with the sports authority, police, fire services and insurers; before a new venue opens, you inspect it yourself. What you say is written into the manual, and the manual sits beside every lifeguard chair.
work: An old lifeguard teaches you to scan: don't watch hands paddling, watch the angle of the head; head tipped back, mouth at the waterline, that's the one about to go under. The next day you spot one in the shallow end.

The test kit shows free chlorine running high, and swimmers say their eyes sting. You go to the plant room to find the water treatment man, and the two of you spend half an hour on the dosing pump readings before turning it down a notch.

A university student taking the deep-water test starts to fall apart at a hundred and fifty meters. You walk the deck beside him until he finishes two hundred, and before signing his certificate you have him tread water for another minute.

On a round of the stadium you find an evacuation route blocked by an advertising company's materials. You photograph it and call on the spot, they come and move it that afternoon, and you close it out in the hazard record.
During a full-hall emergency drill, timing it beside the smoke machine, you notice an exit sign on the second-floor stands isn't lit. The first thing you do after the drill is report it.

A parent complains their child sprained an ankle on a trampoline in the arena. You pull up the camera playback and see two children on one trampoline at once, and hand the footage and your round records to your supervisor.

You do the summer roster: twenty-odd people, one lifeguard for every 250 square meters of pool, extra staff for night sessions. You're at it until one in the morning, and put yourself on the Saturday night session too.

The police review the safety plan for a marathon and ask how you'll control crowd density at the finish. You bring out a map divided into zones, talk for twenty minutes, and he signs the approval form.
A new lifeguard keeps falling short on compression depth in his CPR assessment. You practice with him on the manikin all afternoon, and in the end, dripping with sweat, he passes.

The insurer comes to renew and wants to raise the premium on the strength of last year's three incidents. You lay out how each one was handled and fixed and talk it through, and in the end the rate goes up only a little.

Management wants to cut night-session lifeguards from four to three to save money. At the meeting you lay out attendance data and the staffing standard point by point, and in the end not a single post is cut.

Doing the annual risk assessment, you go through five years of incident and near-miss records and find more than half the slips happened at the door of the same shower room. The next week the floor is replaced.

A newly built city pool is about to open, and you go to inspect it, putting on trunks and swimming a lap along the bottom. When you come up you point out that a stretch of the deep-end wall markings is unclear and require it repainted before opening.

At a sports authority meeting on whether to roll out AI anti-drowning systems at every public pool, you say roll them out, but don't cut a single lifeguard, and then describe the two times the system missed.
A delegation from another province comes to study your venue safety management. You don't take them to the meeting room; you take them to sit by a lifeguard chair for ten minutes and watch the water.
past: In your first year of middle school in Weifang, a sports school coach picks you out: long arms, big feet, good lung capacity. Your father says go, if you make it you'll get into university.
You join the swim team at the sports school in Qingdao, in the water at half past five every morning, ten thousand meters a day, your hair freezing when you climb out in winter.
At the provincial games you come fourth, three tenths of a second short of the provincial team. Your coach pats your shoulder and says nothing.
Your shoulder is injured in training and your times never come back. Your coach says you're at home in the water; go get a lifeguard certificate, and you'll never be short of work.
You pass the national lifeguard qualification and the Red Cross first-aid certificate, doing hundreds of rounds of CPR on the manikin until your wrists ache.
You join this sports center's natatorium as a lifeguard. The first day you climb onto the chair, you find that water looks completely different from above than from inside it.

late.pension_note: Estimate: thirty-odd years of contributions to Qingdao's basic pension for company employees at the sports center's wage base comes to about half your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement you still go to the pool every morning for an early swim. The young man on the chair knows you and says take it slow, Master, and you say I'm not fast.
The neighborhood asks you to talk to primary school children about drowning. You skip the lecture and teach them to float and to shout for help. One child goes home and teaches his grandmother.
Your daughter gets into university to study nursing. She says the first time she did CPR in class, the teacher said her technique was textbook and asked who taught her. She said my dad.
Walking by the sea in summer, you watch a beach lifeguard on the lookout tower, then stand on the sand reading the color of the water, and pick out a rip current.
You look after equipment in the arena and no longer get in the water. Your shoulder gets a little better, and you start walking by the sea every evening.
The young supervisor at the natatorium calls to ask how to roster the summer night sessions, and you go through it with him on the phone, post by post.
When the time comes you retire. Your coworkers give you an old life ring covered in the names of every lifeguard over the years, with yours at the top.
In the first year away from the sports center, whenever you pass any water, pool or sea, your eyes sweep it once first.

You find your footing in the new place. On visits to the sports center your old coworkers say the anti-drowning system has been replaced by a new generation. You ask if they cut lifeguards, and they say no.
The middle-aged man you pulled from the deep end recognizes you on the street one year and insists on treating you to a plate of clams. He says he swims a thousand meters every day now.
Later pools fill with cameras and algorithms, and when a band vibrates someone jumps in. But who saw it first, before that, still takes someone sitting on the chair watching.
Your grandson's first swimming lesson, and you stand at the poolside, eyes on his head the whole time. The coach says don't worry, sir, and you say I'm not worried, and still don't look away.

closing.retire: One summer evening many years later you sit on the rocks by the sea, watching the last swimmers come ashore and the lifeguard on the tower take down the flag. You sit a while longer, until there's no one left on the water, then get up and go home.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find that old life ring covered in names in a cupboard, its colors faded. You wipe it clean and hang it back on the wall.
closing.end: Many years later you pass the sports center, lights on behind the natatorium's glass, a young man on the lifeguard chair. You stand outside a while watching his head turn, sweep after sweep, and then walk on.
